title: Verifier‑Assisted vs. LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier with a bounded automated‑repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven configuration proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 analyzable paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Each pair evaluated the same shared_initial LLM candidate under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation + ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and model, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, limiting observable marginal rescue by the guarded pipeline. We archive execution and analysis artifacts to support replication and motivate follow‑ups varying estimand conditioning, model strength, or repair budget.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. Operational deployment requires semantic pre‑deployment checks because syntactic validity alone can miss sequencing, reachability, and policy constraints that cause outages or security regressions. Prior studies report that generate→validate→repair scaffolds can reduce some errors, but reported effect sizes vary with model capability, task hardness, and validator semantics. To isolate the deterministic rescue effect of a verifier (plus a bounded repair budget) on an identical LLM candidate, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment that conditions the estimand on a single shared_initial candidate per intent. Research question: Does integrating a deterministic verifier into an LLM‑driven change‑generation pipeline increase the probability that an LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation (unflagged) compared with accepting a single‑shot LLM output when both conditions evaluate the same candidate? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300 pairs) conditioning on a single shared_initial candidate to measure verifier/repair rescue utility; (2) artifact‑archived execution and analysis demonstrating a near‑ceiling baseline for the chosen synthetic suite, model, and validator; and (3) evidence‑grounded discussion of estimand interpretation, statistical handling in near‑ceiling regimes, reproducibility details, and operational follow‑ups.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system reports document active research applying LLMs to NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, repair) and propose planner‑centric and tool‑augmented agentic frameworks that enable external validator calls and repair actions. Representative verified themes are: LLMs can produce configuration artifacts across diverse tasks but performance is dataset‑dependent; tool‑augmented pipelines (planner‑centric, ReAct variants) allow validators to check semantics and steer repairs; and generate→validate→repair patterns often improve correctness given sufficient validator coverage. Limitations in prior work include heterogeneous benchmarks, varying validator expressiveness, and few controlled head‑to‑head comparisons that isolate deterministic verifier rescue from scaffold effects. Our study complements this literature by using a preregistered paired estimand that conditions on a single shared_initial candidate, thereby quantifying only the deterministic rescue effect rather than end‑to‑end pipeline benefits from alternative candidate draws or model steering.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered study cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001 prior to confirmatory execution. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) comparing guarded (validator + ≤1 repair) and baseline (accept single‑shot) conditions evaluated on the same shared_initial candidate. Design and frozen choices: declared model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json); validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executing the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule; task suite = synthetic_topology_suite_v1 generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; per‑pair repair budget ≤1 automated repair; one shared_initial model draw per pair; planned analyzable pairs = 300 (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high). Execution contract and stopping: the preregistration specified planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), maximum_model_calls = 600, and a stopping rule requiring halt if >20% dual‑call exclusions occurred. Pilot and sample plan: the preregistration described a pilot (n = 60) to estimate discordance for power calibration; that pilot was not executed (see Disclosure). The main N = 300 was used as pre‑specified with the confirmatory analysis planned as an exact paired McNemar‑equivalent test and paired bootstrap CI.
sections.results: Execution summary and accounting: The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter executed the run from 2026‑08‑30T09:47:41.113164+00:00 to 2026‑08‑30T10:17:21.408465+00:00. Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete_pair_count = 300; failed_episode_count = 0. Provider audit and stage counts (deterministic_reconciliation.json): hosted model calls used = 301 (300 shared_initial + 1 repair), cache_miss_count = 301, shared_initial_generation stage_count = 300, repair stage_count = 1, no failed hosted model calls. Condition margins and contingency: baseline successes = 299/300 (0.9966667), guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Confirmatory inference (paired_binary_analysis_v1): absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (discordant m = n10 + n01 = 1); 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, bootstrap_resamples B = 10000). Rescue diagnostics: a single guarded episode invoked the permitted automated repair and converted a baseline‑flagged candidate into a guarded pass (the lone n10). The archived validator trace for this episode records that the validator detected a must_be_down_for_fields sequencing violation; the automated repair inserted the required 'admin down' sequencing step before the VLAN/MTU change; revalidation returned valid == true. Representative task manifests and full validator traces for rescued episodes are archived (see artifact bundle) and summarized above.
sections.discussion: Statistical interpretation in near‑ceiling regimes: the observed absolute paired improvement (0.00333) is small because single‑shot LLM generation already met validator constraints in 299/300 intents. With only one discordant pair, the exact conditional McNemar test yields p = 1.0, reflecting lack of discordant evidence rather than evidence of no effect. The paired bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01] bounds the plausible paired rescue under the shared_initial estimand to at most 1 percentage point for this experimental context. Estimand conditioning and operational meaning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM draw per intent; it therefore isolates deterministic verifier/repair rescue of that candidate and does not measure verifier benefits that permit independent alternative LLM draws per arm (for example, verifier‑guided resampling or model steering). Organizations choosing to deploy a validator as an audit+repair layer for fixed candidate outputs will find our shared_initial result directly informative; organizations that intend a verifier to actively guide candidate selection require a distinct estimand and experiment. Reproducibility and artifact grounding: all raw outputs, provider traces, task manifests, validator traces, analysis CSVs (condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, missingness_summary.csv, contamination_summary.csv), and logs are archived in the run bundle associated with the preregistration. Execution metadata of interest included model_calls_used = 301, repair stage_count = 1, and the deterministic reconciliation report confirming episode and pair accounting consistency. Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups: (1) when base models are near‑ceiling relative to validator coverage, bounded verifier+repair (shared_initial) yields limited marginal correctness gains but provides deterministic auditing and a targeted repair path for localized sequencing or omission errors; (2) to capture larger pipeline gains, follow‑ups should evaluate independent candidate draws per condition (to assess verifier–model interaction), weaker LLMs or intentionally harder/realistic intents to increase discordance, and expanded repair budgets (iterative repairs or resampling) to quantify repair cost/benefit tradeoffs; (3) evaluation across multiple validators and real production topologies remains necessary to assess external validity.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate (shared_initial) on 300 paired synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Baseline single‑shot generation achieved 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding a small paired improvement (0.00333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). These results show that measured verifier marginality depends strongly on base model capability, task difficulty, validator semantics, and estimand conditioning. We release the preregistration id, execution and analysis artifacts, representative task manifests, and validator traces in the archived run bundle to support replication and motivate follow‑ups that vary estimand choice, model strength, and repair strategies.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator (synthetic_topology_suite_v1); real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.

Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs, larger or smaller models, or different validator implementations and rule sets.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.

Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot (n = 60) intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration recalculation of required sample size was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition.
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may produce different outcomes.
